articles.text: The City of Piedmont will host a virtual Housing Element Community Workshop, the second in a series of community workshops, on Thursday, March 24 at 5:30 p.m. via Zoom. The workshop will focus on the 2023-2031 Housing Element update, and will feature an introduction to the Housing Element draft, which will set forth the city’s goals, policies and actions that address the need for all housing types at various income levels. A complete review and revision of the existing Housing Element must be adopted by Piedmont City Council by December 2023. A highlight of tomorrow’s workshop will be a presentation of a new, interactive digital tool called “The Piedmont Puzzle,” which operates on Balancing Act software. Chris Adams, president and co-founder of Balancing Act, will lead a demonstration on how to use the community tool. It will allow users to pick locations in Piedmont that would be suitable for housing and what that housing might look like. Community members can access the Housing Element workshop by joining the Zoom meeting by computer or smart phone at bit.ly/piedmonthousingpuzzle. You may also call in to the virtual meeting, by dialing (669) 900-9128 and enter webinar meeting number 870 3457 5751. The City installed banners in the center of town and on Grand Avenue in anticipation of upcoming community workshops related to housing equity and the draft Housing Element.
articles.title: Virtual Housing Community Workshop tomorrow at 5:30 p.m.

articles.text: The world knows about the horrors happening in the beautiful country of Ukraine. The world knows of the shelling and the bombing. The world knows of the bullets and blood. Ukraine knows of the war tearing its country apart. But Ukraine also knows of her citizens fighting back against those who invade her country. Ukraine knows the brave souls who give their lives to keep her safe. For the past weeks Ukraine has been defending its territory against the invading Russian forces. With shelling happening all hours of the day and night, many Ukrainians have been forced to take shelter underground – in parking garages, theater basements, and subways – to keep themselves and their loved ones safe. The Ukrainian army, though heavily outnumbered, is holding its ground against the invading Russian forces. Ukraine and Russia have coexisted for centuries without conflict. As a first-generation Russian-American, I remember growing up and watching cartoons based on old Russian legends, always based in Kyiv. I remember when my grandmother who lives in Moscow would come to visit, we would always watch a popular TV show together. The producer of that show is actor-turned Ukrainian president Vladirmir Zelensky. I remember my mother making me Ukrainian borscht and vareniki (dumplings). My life has been influenced by Ukraine in more ways than I can possibly imagine, and I am beyond grateful for it. My parents would always tell me about Russia’s famous writers who hailed from Odessa, Ukraine, and how their works of literature were prized by the entire world. My Jewish father’s grandparents were born near Odessa, and lived there before moving to Moscow. My mother’s Russian relatives still live there. I had always believed that Ukraine and Russia only differed in their language and borders. I still believe to this day that Russians don’t want a war with the people they call their brothers and sisters. I believe it’s the Russian government and its goons who use propaganda and TV to stupify the country. But I speak for myself. I don’t want a war to rip apart countries who are separated by a line drawn on a map.
articles.title: To Ukraine with love, from a Russian-American

articles.text: In the week of March 12-18 only one student COVID case was reported in Piedmont School District, and none by staff members. This was the first week of the new mask policy which highly recommend that they be worn indoors, but no longer requires them. Although Piedmont schools have been very progressive with their vaccination policy and the city of Piedmont has some of the highest vaccination rates in the nation, there have been varying opinions on wearing masks. APT (Piedmont teachers’ union) President Elise Marks teaches English at the high school. She offered the following observation about the first week with the new policy. “I’m not seeing much tension between individuals. People are being respectful [of individual’s choice to wear a mask or not].” “At the same time, I’ve heard from several students who didn’t want to see the mask mandate lifted, that they’re quite uncomfortable having to be in classrooms all day with unmasked people. I’ve had a couple of students choose not to come to school for all or part of this week,” she added. She estimated half to 2/3 of students in her classes are still wearing masks, mostly the N95 or KN95 types. At a school-wide pep rally inside the Binks Rawlings gym on Friday, this reporter observed more than half of students not wearing masks. One week ago, March 16, marked the two-year anniversary of the first COVID stay-at-home order in California. Many in the community are ready to move forward and see mask removal as the next logical step. “I think something that is underserved in our community in Piedmont is the mental health aspect of the pressures we have placed on the children to do things like wear masks, comply with other Covid policies, and be away from schools. As parents, my wife and I do take notice of our kids’ mental welfare as much as their physical welfare and we have concerns there,” said Piedmont alum and parent Jonathan Essner. Alameda county continues to enjoy low COVID numbers, since March 4. The seven-day average since then has hovered between 173 and 113 confirmed daily cases. In the same time period, the seven-day average of daily case counts in the U.S. has decreased from 50,000 to 29,000 daily. Elsewhere, the new subvariant of Omicron BA.2 has caused spikes in case counts across western Europe, a region that has typically been a couple of weeks ahead of the US in showing new COVID trends. On March 18 Germany recorded 300,000 cases. Some scientists are raising the alarm since the number of Americans with booster shots is around 30% while 50-60% of western Europeans have had a booster. On the other side of the world, India’s Bharat Biotech, a vaccine manufacturer, leads the way in the production of a COVID nasal spray vaccine. The argument in favor of this type of vaccine is that it would create antibodies at the point of infection, the nose. In theory this would stop infection before it happens, Piedmont’s Dr. George Rutherford warns of cautious optimism. “It’s a good idea; they may get there someday in the not too distant future. But for right now, I think it is far out on the edge of the horizon.” Rutherford, pointed out that the only current nasal vaccine in the U.S. is for the flu and it doesn’t work for people over 50. It may be hard to administer for very young people since the patient has to breathe in at the same time. “It is not going to do anything unless we can get more than 70% of the population to get it. There is still all the vaccine hesitancy that goes on.” Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: A trip to Disneyland, which begins tomorrow, March 24, is a reward for three years of cookie sales by Piedmont Girl Scouts in Troop 33587. The Scouts, most of whom attend Wildwood Elementary, have sold close to 10,000 boxes of Thin Mints, Samoas and other varieties or cookies since 2020. That volume qualified them for a VIP guided tour of Magic Kingdom. “They’ve been so driven,” said Carolyn Pan, one of the troop leaders. “It’s just amazing how they’ve maintained focus on their goal for so long.” Troop 33587 has been together since 2017 and first set its sights on Disneyland in 2020. They sold more than 5,000 boxes that year before COVID-19 cut the selling season short. Last year, they were only able to sell 1,100 boxes amid pandemic restrictions. Sales have been brisk this year, however. The troop has set up stands throughout Piedmont and Oakland with people lining up to buy in some cases. They also built online stores to take remote orders and knocked on countless doors. “People haven’t seen us for two years,” Pan said. “They’re hungry for cookies.” The 11 girls in the troop have sold an average of 326 boxes each, a number that would be even higher if it wasn’t for supply constraints that limited the number of cookies the Scouts could get. This year, Pan has been struck by how confident the girls are, noting how they project their voices, engage with strangers, and guide customers to flavors with more inventory. “I’ve learned how to manage money and connect with people,” said 10-year-old Junie Waters Worthen, a troop member for the last three years. Cookies are still available online at bit.ly/troop33587, and the Girls Scouts will ship for free any orders over $50 placed on March 26 and 27. To learn more, see their video at https://youtu.be/EOAwwxO7RPo. Lilly Curran sells Girl Scout cookies from the comfort of her car. articles.text: The inaugural Piedmont Food Fest is coming to town. On Sunday, April 24 from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m., in partnership with the city, schools, local businesses, community partners, and fiscal sponsor Social Good, Piedmont Food Fest will welcome visitors and showcase a family-friendly event in Piedmont Park. It will include food, the stories of the people behind the food, as well as multicultural stage performances, locally sourced beer and wine, and a kid activity zone. If all goes well, this event may even turn into another annual tradition the community can look forward to year after year. A central mission of Piedmont Food Fest is to showcase the many diverse offerings of the broader Bay Area that help enrich the experiences of community and neighbors. The event will feature food from Curry Up Now, Ceviche & Co, Swahili Spot, Kiss My Boba, Piedmont’s own Robert Dorsey Catering, and others. There will also be live music from the mariachi duo Son Nuestro, the Great Wall Youth Orchestra, a Black Music Incubator Showcase, and the Oakland Samba Revue. Piedmont Food Fest is open to the public and we encourage attendance from the broader Bay Area. To register or volunteer, please visit www.piedmontfoodfest.org. Early bird deals are available now through March 31. The Food Festival Planning Committee includes Roger Tsai, Diana Lee, Abha Kothari, Kala Hale, Kyle Killion, Tien Teng, David Lau, Amy Kelly, Ellen Moon Lee, Lisa Chan Carnazzo, and Michelle Mazzeo.

articles.text: First field trip for school in two years Millennium High School Principal Shannon Fierro arranged for students to have a field trip – their first in two years – with a work project through Rebuilding Together Oakland on February 18. Students and school staff pitched in to help renovate an historic building in Oakland, now being used for transitional housing for homeless. The renovation team included 50 students and 10 members of the school’s staff and parents. Their work day started at 8:30 a.m. at 722 Washington Street in Oakland. Students gained work experience installing sheetrock, and then preparing and painting several rooms. advisor for the Piedmont Community Service Crew, Fierro was put in touch with Rebuilding Together Oakland, a nonprofit that helps to match groups with projects in the community. The non-profit suggested City Team, an organization that provides transitional housing and wrap-around services for adults transitioning from homelessness, incarceration and substance abuse. City Team is completely renovating an historic building in Old Oakland. “It was fulfilling to do work that actually helps the world,” said MHS 9th grader Nathan Weisz. When completed, the building will offer three meals a day seven days a week, a technology and job center for guest use and housing for over 40 people. MHS students at work on a building renovation: Maile Imburg (left), Ellie Willats, Maddie Hill, Trinity Zamora, Principal Shannon Fierro, Eva Levingston, Megan Foster, Samiya Jones, Grace Rego, and Don Barrett. Millennium High Principal Shannon Fierro (front, left) sits on the bottom step in a hallway of an historic building being renovated by students and staff. Millennium High students in action, painting the interior of City Team’s flagship building which provides transitional housing for the homeless. “I wanted to get students off campus and back out into the world. articles.text: Primitive Data, a FIRST Tech Challenge robotics team with three members from Piedmont, won first place at the NorCal Regionals held on Sunday, March 13 in Sacramento. The Piedmont team was a key player in a three teams winning alliance. Its alliance partners were Kuriosity Robotics from Palo Alto and Quixilver from San Jose. Primitive Data includes Piedmont High seniors Benjamin Colby, Cooper Downing, and Josh Lee, along with Peter Xu from American High in Fremont. A total of 48 teams from Northern California advanced from earlier competitions to qualify for the regionals. In the final showdown, Primitive data and allies defeated an alliance of two teams from Saratoga and one from Folsom. At the NorCal Regionals, Primitive Data rose to the occasion with an effective defensive strategy, frustrating their opponents and complementing the offensive abilities of their alliance partners. An advanced Swerve Drive drivetrain enabled this unique style of play, which required Primitive Data to introduce a number of hardware and software innovations in their robot development. The Primitive Data team was also named the Northern California winner of the FIRST Tech Challenge Innovate Award. “The Innovate Award celebrates a team that thinks outside the box and has the ingenuity, creativity, and inventiveness to make their designs come to life,” explained FIRST Tech. “This judged award is given to the team that has the most innovative and creative robot design solution to any specific components in the FIRST Tech Challenge game. Elements of this award include elegant design, robustness, and ‘out of the box’ thinking related to design.” This was Primitive Data’s first in-person tournament since winning last summer at the Maryland Tech Invitational, an international competition. Their alliance partners then were from Santa Monica and Fremont. Primitive Data was founded by Downing and Colby for the 2020-21 season. A guiding principle of the team is collaboration across boundaries and leadership from students with no adult mentors. With a team of only four members, Primitive Data has successfully competed against teams four times larger and with substantial school resources and professional adult mentorship. The Primitive Data robotics team holds their first-place trophies. Team members include Piedmont High seniors Benjamin Colby (left), Josh Lee, and Cooper Downing, along with Peter Xu, a senior at American High in Fremont.

articles.text: Piedmont police officer Nicole Casalnuovo was promoted to Sergeant on February 19, and received a formal badge pinning ceremony at the March 7 City Council meeting. Specifically, Casalnuovo transitioned from Acting Watch Commander to Sergeant. In her previous role, she earned “bootson-the-ground” experience that prepared her for the promotion. “The transition is pretty seamless. Of course, there are more responsibilities [as Sergeant], but we’re well-prepared at that point,” she explained. “This department works very hard to make sure we’re led in that [upward] direction.” Casalnuovo was hired by the Piedmont Police Department in 2015 as a patrol officer, and eventually assumed the position of juvenile officer in 2019 working in tandem with the school district. As juvenile officer, Casalnuovo worked with Piedmont youth and served as a conduit between the police department, the school administration and faculty. The position was funded by the California Department of Justice Tobacco Grant program. “Ultimately, Nicole was responsible for doing the real work in terms of setting up a new program that had an immense amount of responsibility tied to it. She did an amazing job,” Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers noted at the ceremonial pinning. Casalnuovo’s service to Piedmont youth extends to her role as Advisor to the Piedmont Explorer Post Program, part of the Piedmont Scout Council, that seeks to provide young women and men with the opportunity to explore their interests and aptitudes in the field of law enforcement. Under her tutelage, many Piedmont youth experienced their first “ride-along,” joining Casalnuovo on duty and observing a day in the life of a Piedmont Police Officer. Although the Explorer Post program had to take a backseat the past two years due to COVID, Casalnuovo sought to engage Piedmont youth in other ways. Recently she helped PPD Administrative Assistant April Fitzgerald install a three-shelf “little free library” specifically for young readers ages 3 through 11. The project was created to encourage kids to stop by and Sergeant Nicole Casalnuovo read or borrow a book from the Police Department lobby. Casalnuovo also serves as National Night Out coordinator, one of the largest events hosted by the Department. The event is a community-police awareness-raising “block party,” traditionally held on the first Tuesday of August. Casalnuovo has over 15 years of experience in military and law enforcement. She served as an intelligence and an analyst for the U.S. Air Force before beginning her career in law enforcement. Casalnuovo looks back at her parents and mentor retired Sgt. Grady Joseph of the Central Marin Police Authority, before she receives her ceremonial pin at a March 7 Piedmont City Council meeting. pages.text: Wednesday, March 23, 2022 11 Police Department’s Nicole Casalnuovo promoted to Sergeant By Allyson Aleksey Piedmont police officer Nicole Casalnuovo was promoted to Sergeant on February 19, and received a formal badge pinning ceremony at the March 7 City Council meeting. Specifically, Casalnuovo transitioned from Acting Watch Commander to Sergeant. In her previous role, she earned “bootson-the-ground” experience that prepared her for the promotion. “The transition is pretty seamless. Of course, there are more responsibilities [as Sergeant], but we’re well-prepared at that point,” she explained. “This department works very hard to make sure we’re led in that [upward] direction.” Casalnuovo was hired by the Piedmont Police Department in 2015 as a patrol officer, and eventually assumed the position of juvenile officer in 2019 working in tandem with the school district. As juvenile officer, Casalnuovo worked with Piedmont youth and served as a conduit between the police department, the school administration and faculty. The position was funded by the California Department of Justice Tobacco Grant program. “Ultimately, Nicole was responsible for doing the real work in terms of setting up a new program that had an immense amount of responsibility tied to it. She did an amazing job,” Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers noted at the ceremonial pinning. Casalnuovo’s service to Piedmont youth extends to her role as Advisor to the Piedmont Explorer Post Program, part of the Piedmont Scout Council, that seeks to provide young women and men with the opportunity to explore their interests and aptitudes in the field of law enforcement. Under her tutelage, many Piedmont youth experienced their first “ride-along,” joining Casalnuovo on duty and observing a day in the life of a Piedmont Police Officer. Although the Explorer Post program had to take a backseat the past two years due to COVID, Casalnuovo sought to engage Piedmont youth in other ways. Recently she helped PPD Administrative Assistant April Fitzgerald install a three-shelf “little free library” specifically for young readers ages 3 through 11. The project was created to encourage kids to stop by and Sergeant Nicole Casalnuovo read or borrow a book from the Police Department lobby. Casalnuovo also serves as National Night Out coordinator, one of the largest events hosted by the Department. The event is a community-police awareness-raising “block party,” traditionally held on the first Tuesday of August. Casalnuovo has over 15 years of experience in military and law enforcement. She served as an intelligence and an analyst for the U.S. Air Force before beginning her career in law enforcement. Casalnuovo looks back at her parents and mentor retired Sgt. Grady Joseph of the Central Marin Police Authority, before she receives her ceremonial pin at a March 7 Piedmont City Council meeting. articles.text: Come for the fun, leave with more Summer break is rapidly approaching. As plans come together to fill those 10 weeks, it is time to consider summer camp for your children, not just for the fun they will have, but because they need it now more than ever. When the world is more adult, scary, and sexualized than children are ready for, summer camp is a refuge. Camps across the country believe in embracing childhood, playing outside, and being true to oneself. Those foundations are all very healthy for children, and in today’s world, can be a muchneeded detox. If the idea of a camp cleanse sounds too serious or “woo-woo,” know that reality of summer camp is mostly just heaps of good ol’-fashioned fun. A little secret just between us: fun is the space and the forge that can create the biggest ripples in a camper’s life. • Fun brings campers up to the zip-line platform, but courage takes the leap. • Fun puts ceramic clay into a camper’s hand, but creativity builds the pot. • Fun tries archery, but tenacity gets closer to the bullseye. • Fun pulls campers into the party, but self-assurance dances like no one is watching. • Fun is the brochure, but independence, self-discovery, and exceptional growth is what campers take home. A good couple of weeks at camp is a shield that campers carry into their next year at school. When the world feels like it is closing in, the memories of camp are a touchstone of a more wild and free alternative – a time when they felt truly themselves and can feel that way again. Only summer camp can create that type of fun that leaves you with an unbridled feeling of truth in your soul. Summer camp quiets the noise, and builds a more resilient, empathetic, and open version of yourself. A Camp Augusta camper shows off his aerial skills. old fashioned fun in full force. This summer, consider sending your child to camp, because camp is fun … and so. much. more. articles.text: Dragons’ goalie stops five penalty shots Piedmont girls’ lacrosse coach Carlton Chan’s suffered his team’s first loss in four years to Bishop O’Dowd, a 7-6 down-tothe-wire match last Friday, March 18 at Witter Field. The Highlanders had won the previous six games with its rival. The Highlanders also took a 10-4 loss to Division 1 school Monte Vista at Witter last Tuesday, March 15. It brings the squad to a 1-5 overall record, but despite the bleak standing, Piedmont should handle the rest of its league opponents in the Western Alameda County Conference, and be able to compete for a league championship game against O’Dowd in April “We will see them again in the league playoffs and l already have a few strategies that would hopefully give us an advantage,” said Chan. “We have a tough schedule, but we’re playing like a team... The girls are stepping up,” Chan said. The Highlanders last lost to O’Dowd 10-9 in the 2017 WACC Championship under former coach Emily Hook. This time the Dragons prevented five of penalty shots by Piedmont. Game Recap The Dragons opened with a quick goal in the first minute of play, and Piedmont had a difficult time finding shooting space. Katherine Kinne scored through contact after six minutes – the team’s first clear look at net. Two minutes later, O’Dowd scored its second goal. Piedmont’s Audrey Mahany had a shot on goal with 8:46 left in the first half. PHS broke the scoring drought with six minutes left when Kinne found Elizabeth Ethington on a cut toward the net for a 2-1 O’Dowd lead. Ethington then scored on a wrap around after starting her run from behind the net to make it 2-2 with 2:47 left in the, half. However, O’Dowd scored on its next possession to go ahead 3-2 at halftime. In the second half, Piedmont made it 3-3 when Ethington found Kinne on a pass from behind the net to Kinne cutting in after just 30 seconds. But, once again, BOD answered on its next possession, to edge ahead 4-3. Ethington had a shooting space attempt saved about a minute later, but Molly Ashton swiftly stole the ball from an O’Dowd defender and scooped and scored at with 22:39 left. The Dragons took the faceoff and turned it into another quick score after just 15 seconds, to remain ahead, 5-4. The Dragons’ goalie then stonewalled another shooting space attempt, this time a penalty shot by Mahany with 20 minutes left. O’Dowd then gained possession and scored after one minute, to take its biggest lead of the game at 6-4. The Dragon goalie then made big stops on two more shooting space attempts, another by Mahany and one by Kinne with 16:20 left in the game. Ruby Guzdar broke Piedmont’s scoring drought after weaving around two defenders, to bring the score to 6-5 with 13 minutes left. O’Dowd scored its final goal with 5:37 left in the game. articles.text: Piedmont’s baseball team defeated non-league Skyline 5-2 on Tuesday, March 15 at home, but lost on the road to Alameda 4-3 on Wednesday, March 16 and Berkeley 6-3 at home on Friday, March 18. articles.text: The tide seems to have changed in the world of lacrosse. With Greg Gately and other former lacrosse stars now in college, the Piedmont boys’ lacrosse team suffered a 13-7 loss to Bishop O’Dowd on March 18 at the Dragons’ home field. It marked O’Dowd’s first win over the Highlanders since April 2017, a string of six games. “O’Dowd had a really good defense, they are hyper aggressive with a lot of seniors. They took it to us in the first and second quarter. We made a good push in the third, and never stopped trying. We showed a lot of heart, but it was atypical of Piedmont lacrosse,” said first year coach Alex Yu, who was an assistant with BOD when they last defeated PHS ’17. O’Dowd’s defense performed as good as advertised with frequent pressing and forcing a wide field to keep an eye on Piedmont’s cutters moving toward the net. “We had a lot of solo-dodges into multiple defenders and never got settled. Give credit to them and their defense,” said Yu. The match was Piedmont’s first league game of the season. The Dragons were very physical with checks and shoulder chargers, committing 10 penalties. PHS was able to score only three times on penalty plays. Prior to the game, O’Dowd seniors could be heard reminding teammates of last spring’s 9-8 overtime Piedmont win. “O’Dowd has a tough defense and they like to push out a lot. Next game, I think we need to capitalize with off-ball movement and more cutting, that’s the one thing we can counter with when they are pushing us out. We can do better in transition as well,” said junior leader Jack Nelson. “They had more ground ball possession than us and it took a while to figure out what worked. We [need to] get more consistent and get more ground balls,: said junior Soren Dixon. Game Recap The Dragons opened with four consecutive goals until Nathan Fredericks flicked a pass to Soren Dixon for a goal with 2:42 left in the first quarter on a 2-man advantage. Dixon made it 4-2 while up a man as well with 1:25 to go, when he stole the ball from BOD goalie Alex Sproul, who charged out of net after recording a save against Dixon. The Highlanders also started the second quarter with a man-advantage, but Dixon and Fredericks were stonewalled by the goalie. BOD then scored four consecutive goals again to jump ahead 9-2 with 42 seconds left until halftime. Rylan Nelson launched in a goal with 10 seconds on the clock for a 9-3 halftime score. In the third quarter, Piedmont drew a penalty 30 seconds in and attempted a wrap-around shot by Dixon, but his shot was saved. O’Dowd committed another penalty with 6:59 to go and Fredericks fired another shot on target, but the keeper was there to thwart his attempt again. At the 5:45 mark, Fredericks found the net on a low-arching shot to make it 9-4, but O’Dowd scored 19 seconds later, 10-4. From there, PHS added three consecutive goals, but the die was cast. Spencer Settlemier scored after scooping a ground ball in the attacking area and quickly flicking it into the net with 4:45 left in the third, 10-5. The Highlanders then converted a man-advantage with 52 seconds to spare when Dixon found Jack Nelson for a goal, 10-6. In the fourth quarter, Fredericks fed Rylan Nelson for a goal with 9:45 left in the game to make it 10-7. O’Dowd scored three more times for the 13-7 final. Ben McMurtry led the team in rushing. The key to the team’s success was its defense led by Kellin de Verney who was matched against the opponents’ best receivers all season. articles.text: San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) is hosting an exhibition of artist Tauba Auerbach’s interdisciplinary works. Auerbach, born in 1981 in San Francisco, creates work that considers the ways that structure, pattern, and gesture function from intricate to vast scales. A life-long student of mathematics and physics, she uses a variety of media, ranging from painting and photography to book design and musical performance. In her first solo exhibition, Auerbach showed a series of text-based drawings that explored various linguistic systems that included calligraphy, Morse code, semaphore signals, the Ugaritic alphabet and Alexander Melville Bell’s visible speech. The title of the exhibition, “S v Z”, is a reference to the close yet indeterminate relationship between form and meaning that surfaces throughout the artist’s materials. articles.text: March 25 concert includes Peter and the Wolf with Wendy McNaughton as narrator Celebrating its 50th year, Berkeley Symphony will perform a concert this Friday, March 25 at 7:30 p.m. at First Congregational Church of Berkeley at 2330 Durant Avenue. The program includes a uniquely Berkeley retelling of Sergei Prokofiev’s Peter and the Wolf, narrated by illustrator and graphic journalist Wendy MacNaughton, and Maurice Ravel’s Mother Goose Suite. Audio descriptions will be provided for Peter and the Wolf, as three local illustrators bring the music and story to life through live drawings during the performance. MacNaughton has a long history of combining the practice of deep looking, listening and drawing to create stories of often overlooked people, places and things. As the creator and host of “DrawTogether,” a participatory drawing show for kids, she helps others use art to bolster social-emotional skills, self-confidence and connection. Tickets that include audio descriptions of Peter and the Wolf are $30 and are available at berkeleysymphony.org or by calling the box office at 510.841.2800. Please mention ACCESSWOLF30 when booking. A special feature will be the appearance of Hindustani singer Saili Oak and soprano Maya Kherani performing Indian-American composer Reena Esmail’s Meri Sakhi Ki Avaazi, a cross-cultural journey that explores family and community. Esmail works between the worlds of Indian and Western classical music. Berkeley Symphony requires proof of vaccination and masks to be worn at all in-person events. articles.text: Some dining traditions have served us well over the years. Anyone from New Orleans knows that Monday is reserved for red beans and rice. In many places, tamales are served on Tuesdays. And Fridays were reserved for fish. You might think that this was entirely a Catholic tradition, but that is not entirely correct. Both Catholics as well as other Christians, and Jews avoided meat on Fridays. The reasons were completely different, but the result was identical. In both cases, Friday was a holy day. This word was spelled “haly”. The species of flat fish were termed “butte”. By combining these two words we get halibut. Here is a festive fish recipe from Liguria, Italy which you can enjoy on Fridays or any other day. It combines fish, any type of pasta and fennel. I tried the recipe with potato gnocchi, but I would suggest using some type of spaghetti. For four people, make a circle with your thumb and middle finger. That is enough pasta for four people. Plan on a quarter pound of fish per person. The traditional recipe uses lobster tails but you can also use crab claws. I used rock shrimp and it was terrific. Do not use clams or mussels. If you want to avoid shellfish, I would suggest using a firm fleshed fish such as Corvina sea bass or rock cod. Swordfish is also a good choice. articles.text: If you happen to have kids hanging out at your house and you walk by a room and see a youngster/tween/teen stretched out on a bed or sofa reading a comic book, take a moment and consider what that means. Begin with the word “reading.” Then pause and see if you can get a look at the cover. What’s the art look like? What or who is the title character? Then with all the humility and approbation you can muster, ask, “Whatcha reading?” With that question, mom or dad, you’ve entered hallowed ground. When I was a youngster, I yearned to learn to read. I spent time with my “cousins” who were slightly older and had stacks of comics in their rooms, magazines that I paged through but couldn’t decode. .I soon read comic books voraciously, willingly suspending my disbelief, spending countless Saturdays in comic book trades with other comic book fans. All of us were collectors of a sort and each of us had a favorite superhero. Keep in mind that we arrived at the tail end of what is now thought of as the “Golden Age” of comics. Superman, for example, was created in 1938 and had already established a legacy of fighting for truth and justice and the American way. Ditto Captain Marvel, though later. Each comic – most by created DC and Marvel Comics – was made up of sequential panels with text in boxes and dialogue in balloons, highlighted by drawings that were vibrant, kinetic, and compelling In the aggregate they told a story of peril and adventure. And there were, of course, the characters that included the world of Disney (Mickey, Donald, Pluto, Goofy and so on) as well as a sprawling cast of superheroes such as Superman, Batman and Robin, Spider-Man, Aquaman, and Wonder Woman. It was a world of richness, imagination, and endless permutations. It wasn’t until the 1970s when Marvel Comics created a stable of superheroes, assembled by the hugely creative team of illustrators Stan Lee and Jack Kirby. They were initially called the Fantastic Four: Ant-man, the Hulk, Iron Man, and Thor and later the Wasp and Captain America. Gradually the Marvel Universe of superheroes grew deeper and wider, with a rotating roster. Soon came The Avengers, whose motto was that the Avengers “fight the foe no single hero can withstand.” In 2012, Marvel Studios (now owned by Disney) created the first live-action feature titled Avengers and introduced to worldwide audiences this rich cast of superheroes. It had a seismic opening box office weekend. In 2015 came Avengers: Age of Ultron, and, in 2016, the cohort made an appearance in Captain America: Civil War, followed by Avengers: Infinity War in 2018. The number of characters has expanded exponentially, and when the sequel to Infinity War, Avengers: End Game, opened, super fans (and parents sitting several rows back), likely needed a program for the mind-numbing layers of characters. Keep an eye out for a genetically engineered raccoon called Rocket who is one smart, highly verbal bounty hunter. Keep in mind that all of the ideas began with a pulpy magazine called a comic book that appeared in 1933, based on humorous panels (comics) that were lifted from newspapers. The rest is history. And in the world of comics, “reading” is still the operative word. Buy a few and leave them in the living room and see what happens... Just a suggestion.
articles.title: Deconstructing the Comic Book

pages.text: Wednesday, March 23, 2022 21 Deconstructing the Comic Book By Chris Honoré If you happen to have kids hanging out at your house and you walk by a room and see a youngster/tween/teen stretched out on a bed or sofa reading a comic book, take a moment and consider what that means. Begin with the word “reading.” Then pause and see if you can get a look at the cover. What’s the art look like? What or who is the title character? Then with all the humility and approbation you can muster, ask, “Whatcha reading?” With that question, mom or dad, you’ve entered hallowed ground. When I was a youngster, I yearned to learn to read. I spent time with my “cousins” who were slightly older and had stacks of comics in their rooms, magazines that I paged through but couldn’t decode. .I soon read comic books voraciously, willingly suspending my disbelief, spending countless Saturdays in comic book trades with other comic book fans. All of us were collectors of a sort and each of us had a favorite superhero. Keep in mind that we arrived at the tail end of what is now thought of as the “Golden Age” of comics. Superman, for example, was created in 1938 and had already established a legacy of fighting for truth and justice and the American way. Ditto Captain Marvel, though later. Each comic – most by created DC and Marvel Comics – was made up of sequential panels with text in boxes and dialogue in balloons, highlighted by drawings that were vibrant, kinetic, and compelling In the aggregate they told a story of peril and adventure. And there were, of course, the characters that included the world of Disney (Mickey, Donald, Pluto, Goofy and so on) as well as a sprawling cast of superheroes such as Superman, Batman and Robin, Spider-Man, Aquaman, and Wonder Woman. It was a world of richness, imagination, and endless permutations. It wasn’t until the 1970s when Marvel Comics created a stable of superheroes, assembled by the hugely creative team of illustrators Stan Lee and Jack Kirby. They were initially called the Fantastic Four: Ant-man, the Hulk, Iron Man, and Thor and later the Wasp and Captain America. Gradually the Marvel Universe of superheroes grew deeper and wider, with a rotating roster. Soon came The Avengers, whose motto was that the Avengers “fight the foe no single hero can withstand.” In 2012, Marvel Studios (now owned by Disney) created the first live-action feature titled Avengers and introduced to worldwide audiences this rich cast of superheroes. It had a seismic opening box office weekend. In 2015 came Avengers: Age of Ultron, and, in 2016, the cohort made an appearance in Captain America: Civil War, followed by Avengers: Infinity War in 2018. The number of characters has expanded exponentially, and when the sequel to Infinity War, Avengers: End Game, opened, super fans (and parents sitting several rows back), likely needed a program for the mind-numbing layers of characters. Keep an eye out for a genetically engineered raccoon called Rocket who is one smart, highly verbal bounty hunter. Keep in mind that all of the ideas began with a pulpy magazine called a comic book that appeared in 1933, based on humorous panels (comics) that were lifted from newspapers. The rest is history. And in the world of comics, “reading” is still the operative word. Buy a few and leave them in the living room and see what happens... Just a suggestion. articles.text: Renée Zellweger as Judy Garland in Judy. After a brief flashback in which Louis B. Mayer is lecturing young Frances Gumm (later to be known worldwide as Judy Garland), the film Judy, released in 2019, opens with Judy and her two children returning late at night to her L.A. hotel where – her suitcases at her feet, her exhaustion palpable – she is told that her suite has been released to someone else and her things have been put in storage. Her line of credit, she’s told, has been cancelled. Desperate, broke, with bills in arrears, she takes the children to their father, Sid Luft (Rufus Sewel), where she leaves them and quickly signs to do a series of shows in a London nightclub, Talk of the Town. Its owner (Michael Gambon), has warily made a bet that the audience will indeed turn out to see this still famous entertainer and that Judy will perform as promised. Just to be sure, however, she is assigned an assistant (Jesse Buckley) to shadow her days and remind her of the daily schedule, for they are ever cognizant that this once huge talent may have reached her nadir. And so, all those who satellite the show’s preparation watch and wait for any hint of Judy faltering. The movie audience knows her story all too well known, if only in outline form. The London performances represent a fragile opportunity, desperate to find something to slow her fall from the limelight. The film walks a precarious tightrope. In every scene and with every decision, the heartfelt wish is that she will prevail. But simultaneously, we know that this will not end well. And yet we hope, even when she refuses to rehearse, when she washes down pills with alcohol, when she suffers chronic insomnia, when she shows up late, often overcome with a stage fright, as her audience waits. These emotions are not simply the result of a known foreshadowing, but testimony to the transcendent performance by actress Renée Zellweger. Absent from movies for almost a decade, she embraces the character of Judy as if she stepped into a holographic figure and uses all of her own gifts to bring Judy back to us. Zellweger is that good. It is her voice we hear. It is her commitment to this performance that she offers without hesitation. And as she sits at the end of the stage and the lights wash over her, singing “Somewhere Over the Rainbow,” she heartbreakingly dazzles. It’s a breathtaking moment. Using flashbacks, we observe young Judy (still Frances) following a yellow brick road, every stone laid by cynical and avaricious adults, such as Louis B. Mayer, and most certainly her uber-stage mother who plied her with stay awake/diet drugs and relentless admonishments (“look at the birthday cake, don’t eat it”), while obliterating her youth. From the first frame of this remarkably well-told story, it is a tragedy in the making. And it is also a window into the price of fame and those pursuing it know how imperfect that yellow brick road can be. One of the final lines, part of the ending credits, tells us that six months after Judy left London she died. She was 47. Zellweger did win an Oscar for Best Leading Actress for her outstanding portrayal Judy. Directed by Rupert Goold. With Renée Zellweger, Jessie Buckley, Finn Wittrock, Rufus Sewell, and Michael Gambon. Released in 2019. 1 hr., 58 min. Rated PG-13. Now streaming on Prime. articles.text: In its many extraordinary films over the years, Pixar (now Pixar/Disney) has focused on countless emotional issues: in Inside Out it emphasized that sadness was necessary to experience joy; in Coco it examined how love can prevail after death; and in WALL-E how greed can overwhelm humanity. But it’s in the wonderful, coming-of-age animated feature Turning Red that Pixar courageously, and with sensitivity, tackles the issue of female puberty. Re-released this year (2022), the story, set in Toronto, has at its center a 13-year-old girl named Meilin Lee (Rosalie Chang). She plays the flute, is an eighth grade honor student, and in all respects an ideal girl on the cusp of becoming a young woman. But despite all of her accomplishments, she finds herself rebelling against the strict rules of her over-controlling mother, Ming (Sandra Oh), the quintessential helicopter mom. We soon learn that when Meilin becomes emotional (some teens might describe this as getting your freak on), and is overwhelmed by feelings that seem beyond her understanding – perhaps set in motion by, well, a boy-band, or a store clerk that she’s crushing on – she turns into a very large red panda, a character that is symbolic of the stress and roller coaster ride known as adolescence. The repercussions of Meilin’s first period, an example of all the changes she’s going through, are handled with sensitivity, certainly within the parameters of the film’s PG limits, and there’s not a gratuitous moment in this nicely told tale. The story does convey that puberty, this tumultuous rite of passage, is a beast, a composite of seemingly unbearable stress and self-conscious emotions that define this time in an adolescent female’s life. Meilin quickly learns that all she has to do is calm down, and she will revert from the giant red panda back into herself, the ideal student and newbie teen that her parents so warmly love. But we also see that Meilin struggles with her feelings of ambivalence regarding being the compliant and obedient daughter or pushing back against her mother, however timidly. The question posed throughout is, does she want to conform to the rules? She is surrounded by Chinese culture and caring parents. But despite her supportive family, Meilin’s ultimate preference is her influential peer group, composed of Miriam (Ava Morse), Priya (Maitreyl Ramakrishman), and Abby (Hyein Park) who are never put off by Meilin’s alter ego panda. In fact, they devise a plan to sell tickets to their school classmates, which will allow them to watch her transform into the giant red panda. The girls’ plan is to use the proceeds to attend a concert by their favorite boy-band 4*Town, whose songs are reminiscent of boy-bands like ‘N-Sync. When Meilin asks permission to go, her parents are, naturally, hesitant, knowing that such concerts create intense, even frenzied emotions, and Ming is fearful that her daughter will “go all red panda.” But Meilin comes to understand that her red panda is an integral part of who she is, however disconcerting those moments might be. Turning Red is filled with teachable moments in the best Pixar tradition, with one overriding lesson: be yourself. Pixar nails it. Turning Red. Directed by Domee Shi. A Pixar animated film. Released in 2022. With voices of Rosalie Chang, Sandra Oh, Ava Morse. 1 hr., 40 min. PG-13. Now streaming on Disney.

The walkers took a short side trip up Cambrian Avenue so hey could walk down a 104-foot, hidden path between Cambrian and St. James. It is an old short cut between the streets and doesn’t have handrails. At the end of St. James is Corpus Christi Church at the corner of Park Boulevard. The walkers decided to continue onto Leimert Boulevard. On the Leimert bridge that spans a canyon is a plaque that tells its history. Its official name is the Sausal Creek Arch Bridge which was completed in 1926. George Posey, Alameda County Surveyor and engineer of the Posey Tube between Oakland and Alameda, designed it. It is 257 feet long and 118 feet high. The Park Boulevard Company, which was owned by Walter and Harry Leimert, was responsible for building it and running a Key System streetcar line across it. The Leimerts wanted to develop an Oakmore Highlands neighborhood on the other side of the canyon. The bridge, with distant views of San Francisco, spans Dimond Canyon far below, and was originally part of Antonio Maria Peralta’s land grant. There was once extensive lumbering in the area with great redwoods cut and floated down the creek to Lake Merritt and the Bay. The walkers explored the retail block beyond the bridge, where Rocky’s Market, is the centerpiece. It was founded in 1961 and sells local, organic produce and other items. Noemi Alvarado also shared that at the end of the block, up Arden Place, is a trail that goes up to Highway 13. It was getting close to noon, and time for the walkers to return to Piedmont’s town center. It ended up being almost a five-mile walk, one of the group’s longer walks, but on a beautiful morning with unexpected history. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation is required at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu.

articles.text: Last week a robust group of 35 members of the Walking on Wednesdays group showed up for a long journey on St. James Drive – to Park Boulevard and back. It was noted that the next day was St. Patrick’s Day. A little research had found that Saint Patrick was a fifth-century Romano-Christian missionary and bishop in Ireland and is the primary patron saint of Ireland. Saint Patrick’s Day is observed on March 17. The walkers felt they could walk St. James Drive, the only Piedmont street that references a saint. Research showed that St. James was one of the Twelve Apostles of Jesus, and was one of the first disciples to join Jesus. He and his brother John were with their father by the seashore when Jesus called them to follow him and be “fishers of men.” St. James was also the first to be martyred according to the New Testament. He died in 44 AD and is the patron saint of Spain. Piedmont’s St. James Drive was named after St. James Woods, an early, very large Piedmont neighborhood development. St. James Drive is .7 of a mile and is lovely, flat, and easy to walk. Additionally, at its end on Park Boulevard, there were options for the walkers to continue on. They could either see Cavendish Lane, an Oakland street with four homes with Piedmont addresses, or cross Park Boulevard to the Leimert Bridge and a few retail stores. They went past Crocker Park on Hampton to its intersection with St. James Drive, where this street starts. One block further at La Salle Avenue are two large columns that marked one of the entrances to the St. James Woods development. The group noted that the columns are still missing lanterns on their tops. Mike Henn remembered a few years ago the neighbors wanted the City to install new ones, but the City didn’t have the money to do it, so it never happened. He and his brother John were with their father by the seashore when Jesus called them to follow him and be “fishers of men.” St. James was also the first to be martyred according to the New Testament. He died in 44 AD and is the patron saint of Spain. Piedmont’s St. James Drive was named after St. James Woods, an early, very large Piedmont neighborhood development. St. James Drive is .7 of a mile and is lovely, flat, and easy to walk. Additionally, at its end on Park Boulevard, there were options for the walkers to continue on. They could either see Cavendish Lane, an Oakland street with four homes with Piedmont addresses, or cross Park Boulevard to the Leimert Bridge and a few retail stores. They went past Crocker Park on Hampton to its intersection with St. James Drive, where this street starts. One block further at La Salle Avenue are two large columns that marked one of the entrances to the St. James Woods development. The group noted that the columns are still missing lanterns on their tops. Mike Henn remembered a few years ago the neighbors wanted the City to install new ones, but the City didn’t have the money to do it, so it never happened. The walkers also noted the distinctive four brown tiles that are inlayed in each section of the concrete sidewalks on the length of St. James Drive. The walkers took a short side trip up Cambrian Avenue so hey could walk down a 104-foot, hidden path between Cambrian and St. James. It is an old short cut between the streets and doesn’t have handrails. At the end of St. James is Corpus Christi Church at the corner of Park Boulevard. The walkers decided to continue onto Leimert Boulevard. On the Leimert bridge that spans a canyon is a plaque that tells its history. Its official name is the Sausal Creek Arch Bridge which was completed in 1926. George Posey, Alameda County Surveyor and engineer of the Posey Tube between Oakland and Alameda, designed it. It is 257 feet long and 118 feet high. The Park Boulevard Company, which was owned by Walter and Harry Leimert, was responsible for building it and running a Key System streetcar line across it. The Leimerts wanted to develop an Oakmore Highlands neighborhood on the other side of the canyon. The bridge, with distant views of San Francisco, spans Dimond Canyon far below, and was originally part of Antonio Maria Peralta’s land grant. There was once extensive lumbering in the area with great redwoods cut and floated down the creek to Lake Merritt and the Bay. The walkers explored the retail block beyond the bridge, where Rocky’s Market, is the centerpiece. It was founded in 1961 and sells local, organic produce and other items. Noemi Alvarado also shared that at the end of the block, up Arden Place, is a trail that goes up to Highway 13. It was getting close to noon, and time for the walkers to return to Piedmont’s town center. It ended up being almost a five-mile walk, one of the group’s longer walks, but on a beautiful morning with unexpected history. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation is required at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. articles.text: Dear Jim: Now that we are working from home full time, and one of our adult children is moving in after college, we are considering digging out our basement for more space. Is this a good option for our home? With the new post-pandemic work-at-home reality, coupled with the explosion in home values, our company has seen a marked increase in requests for basement projects in the past few years. These jobs are proving to be great solutions to create new space, but there are several things to consider before turning this dream into a reality. Is it the best option for creating new space? Most homeowners have three possibilities to add new living space, each with advantages and disadvantages. A new addition behind your home is the simple, more affordable approach but requires sufficient space to do it, limited by an (average) allowed lot coverage of less than 50% and property line setbacks. A second-floor addition will add possible warmth, light, and views, but will likely require structural work below, neighbor buy-in and is pricier. A new basement offers cooler living space and is easiest to permit. However, potential lack of views, windows and light need to be considered. Basement renovations can lead to unexpected work Basement jobs typically consist of three elements-the structural work and dig out, the remodel, and what I call the infrastructure project. New foundations, drainage and digging down to create an 8’ ceiling are basic considerations. Then, often a substantial portion of the utilities need to be upgraded since they are outdated, insufficient for the increased space and need to be placed in a centralized location to accommodate the new floor plan. If you have an old foundation, drainage and seismic issues, plus outdated utilities, this may be the perfect fit. What are the limitations on what new spaces can be added? Access and windows are often the two most important things to consider. Depending on the slope of your property, the location and size of windows can be limited. 12-foot tall ceilings on this project required significant rebar and waterproofing. If you are looking for internal access, you will need to carve out the space upstairs to add a stairway- otherwise you would be limited to an outside entrance. For added bedroom spaces you will need enough height for an egress window (usually around 4’ minimum), so that may be a consideration. He is a long-time Piedmont resident and has been doing structural repair and basement renovation in local neighborhoods since 1983. articles.text: Sign at entrance I have been enchanted by Tiki style restaurants since my family frequented one called The Islands in my childhood in Phoenix, Arizona. Twenty years ago when I moved to the Bay Area, we celebrated our relocation with a family dinner at Trader Vic’s in Emeryville. So here I was all these years later being escorted into the small private dining room in the back of the restaurant to have lunch with General Manager Faith Nebergall and conduct an interview. Faith relocated to the Bay Area from Chicago and got her first job here as a cocktail waitress at Trader Vic’s. She worked her way up through the organization and is now General Manager of the Emeryville flagship restaurant. Trader Vic’s has deep roots in the East Bay. The chain had its beginnings when “Trader” Vic Bergeron started a restaurant in the 1930’s called Hinky Dinks on San Pablo Avenue in Oakland. Inspired by the success of Don the Beachcomber tiki restaurants in LA and Chicago, he changed the name to Trader Vic’s and opened a location in San Francisco on Cosmo Place that became one of the city’s iconic restaurants. In 1972 Bergeron opened a new spacious restaurant right on the water at the marina in Emeryville. The company expanded rapidly with restaurants in Seattle, Chicago, Atlanta, Beverly Hills, Scottsdale and many more including their first international location in London. While today there are only three Trader Vic’s in the U.S. – Emeryville, Atlanta and the San Jose airport – the company began franchising locations in a number of exotic locations and now have restaurants in Dubai, Qatar, United Arab Emirates, Oman, Bahrain, Jordan and the Seychelles Islands. Vic Bergeron was a pioneer, and it can be said that it was the first “fusion” restaurant decades before that style became trendy. To this day the menu blends Polynesian, Chinese, Thai and European elements. We started with the Cosmo Tidbits which is a pupu platter of assorted appetizers – crispy shrimp, braised marinated pork, crunchy wontons and BBQ spareribs. We also sampled the Trader Vic’s salad with Javanese dressing and the tuna poke made with big chunks of fresh ahi. In addition, we had fried rice with shrimp, chili coconut chicken which was a fresh tasting stir fry, and a Hawaiian Cubana sandwich which had the original sliced pork and cheese plus fresh pineapple. It took me right back to the delicious Cuban spots I used to haunt when I lived in Miami. The menu changes several times a year but the classics remain. (Bongo Bongo soup has fallen out of favor). One of the most distinctive aspects of TV’s culinary style is the use of two huge Chinese wood-fired ovens. They sit in the middle of the restaurant behind glass to protect from the smoke but so everybody can see the cooks lowering big racks of spareribs and whole ducks into the ovens. The item I have ordered most over the years is the oven cooked Chinese duck. It has delicious crispy skin and tender succulent meat with aromas of hoisin and Chinese 5 spice powder – totally delicious. (The ovens don’t operate during the lunch shift.) But Trader Vic’s is more than about the food – it’s the experience. Here is how Steve Siegelman, author of “Trader Vic’s Tiki Party” describes it. “You walked out of your life and into that swank, clubby Polynesian fantasy world, blinking as your eyes adjusted to the dim light, and slowly took it all in. There were carved tiki heads, spears, and tribal drums competing for space with ship’s bells, fishing nets, shark jawbones, and harpoons. Overhead, outrigger canoes floated among the rafters above a jungle of bamboo, palms, and Technicolor flora. “Here and there purple flames flickered under platters of pupus. Over by the massive clay oven, a chef was fishing meat from the roaring fire with a long iron hook. The Hawaiian-shirted bartenders were turning out concoctions of equal parts rum and Hollywood spectacle – a Kamaaina in a ceramic coconut, a two-quart Rum Keg with four impossible long straws, a hurricane glass sporting a garland of island fruit and flowers crowned with a winking plaster parrot. “And all of it – the drinks, the food, the laughter, the carefully crafted chaos of the tropical Trader Vic’s dining room. The bar at Trader Vic’s. Manager Faith Nebergall and the Potted Parrot. décor – came together to create an irresistible mix of excitement, sophistication, and over-thetop fun. From the moment you walked in, you felt like you were on vacation on a faraway island somewhere outside of time, at a perfectly orchestrated party.” Now we come to the most important thing about Trader Vic’s – THE DRINKS! Vic Bergeron is most famous for inventing the Mai Tai. One day he was behind the bar and he grabbed some J.Wray and Nephew rum, lime juice, sugar syrup, orange curacao and a little French orgeat, mixed them together with ice and handed one to some friends visiting from Tahiti. After a sip they declared “It’s mai tai roa ae!”– Tahitian for “Out of this world!” And thus, the Mai Tai was born. It is to this day the most popular drink at Trader Vic’s and they have two versions – the Original, and the “SF” with an extra float of rum on top. Faith Nebergall informed me that one of the most popular drinks is not even on the menu, but insiders know to order the Tiki Puka Puka cocktail. Why so popular? It is the strongest drink they make, using four different rums. I followed that with the Suffering Bastard, a drink from the Sheppards Hotel in Cairo. Another popular tiki drink is the Zombie, hyped by the fact that the menu used to warn customers that only two per person were allowed. Also recommended are the Potted Parrot “when it’s time to go home the parrot goes with you,” the Samoan Fog Cutter “strong enough to cut through any fog and later put you in one!” and Tiki Grog “warning more than one may result in a temporary tiki face.” The restaurant also carries a Founder Vic Bergeron pretty good wine selection but oddly the Cabernet-heavy list is more appropriate for a midwestern steak house than a tiki joint. But to me the wine list is beside the point. You can get good wine anywhere …where else can you get great tiki drinks like these? The bottom line is 85 years after Trader Vic started his little restaurant on San Pablo Ave. in Oakland the brand is going strong. On a recent Friday evening when I stopped in with friends for a drink, I was delighted to find the large dining room packed with diners and the bar equally hopping. So it looks like this venerable institution has made it through the pandemic and is heading into the future in search of the next million Mai Tais.

pages.text: Wednesday, March 23, 2022 27 Dear Abby A pet column compiled by Piedmont pets Aggressive dogs should avoid dog parks By Abby, a Bernese Mountain Dog Dear Abby: We found a small pug wandering around the parking lot of Trader Joe’s in Emeryville. We took her to the Vet but she was not chipped and was not wearing a collar. The Vet said she was only a puppy, under a year old, less than 15 pounds. We’ve named her Noqui which is Spanish for Gnocci. So far no one has responded to the Lost & Found post that we put online on Craig’s List and Nextdoor. We’d love to find her owners. Come over and meet her, or I’ll come to you. -Natalia noqui2022@gmail.com Dear Natalia, The Pug Queen tells me that you should post ASAP on Pug Rescue of NorCal at Pugpros.org. It is a non-profit which many pug owners know about and search. It is also smart to call the Piedmont and Emeryville Police Departments and let them know you found a Pug pup. Hundreds of plants have been stolen and the Oakland Police do not have the time to watch the garden because they’re pretty busy. Please tell all your dog buddies to be on alert if they’re in the neighborhood and out for a walk. In this day of turmoil, we need our rose garden to restore us. articles.text: Old World elegance and a modern lifestyle come together in the 1918 Jacobethan Revival estate at 456 Wildwood Avenue in Piedmont. Recently refurbished, this 6++ bedroom, 7++ bathroom grand estate was designed by Albert Farr with a wealth of architectural details. As you pass through the wrought iron gate and stone pillars, the prominent parapeted gables topped with finials and tall angled bays with leaded glass windows dominate the façade. The stone driveway encircles a fountain and brings you to the richly paneled entry doors, recessed in a Tudor arch. In true Albert Farr fashion, the wood paneled foyer opens to handsome rooms. Farr’s one slogan in designing a building was, “Do the job right. Please the client, but do it right.” Many would agree that Farr designed this house “right.” The grand foyer with its gleaming gumwood paneling extends from a spacious living room on the west to the elegant dining room. The tones of the ornate Italianate ceiling set the color for adjacent rooms. Paneled walls cleverly conceal the doors to the powder room, coat closet and elevator, now a closet. Oak flooring in a herringbone parquet pattern runs throughout the main floor. Three sets of leaded glass French doors open to a rear terrace, overlooking lush gardens and pool. Balustrades line the terrace and the steps down to the lawn. The swimming pool was replaced by a pool with an integrated spa. Leaded glass French doors open to the spacious living room which fills the western end of the house. Four bay windows bring in natural light, and French doors open to a terrace. The blue walls relate to the blue of the ornate ceiling in the foyer. Mirrored French doors open to the dining room with its chandelier, decorative plaster ceiling, and bay window overlooking the terrace, lawn and pool. The red tinted walls recall the red of the ceiling in the foyer. The façade of the home at 456 Wildwood Avenue designed in 1918 by Albert Farr, the architect who designed Piedmont’s City Hall and Piedmont Community Church. A newspaper clipping from Architect and Engineer magazine shows a photo of the Albert Farr designed house at 456 Wildwood Avenue in 1918, the year it was built. In 1930, the house was owned by industrialist Bert Scott, who had a Christmas Tree by the fountain in the entry courtyard. The wood-paneled grand foyer at 456 Wildwood Avenue extends for much of the ground floor. The chef’s kitchen has been enlarged and remodeled with new slate counter tops, coffered ceiling, and a large central island. French doors open to the pool area and nearby outdoor dining area. The breakfast room offers a pleasant space for casual family dining. The grand staircase fills the two-story, leaded-glass bay and is accented with shields of colored glass, a grand chandelier and polished wood. This staircase accesses the three main floors of the house. A second, utility stairway extends to all four floors. Upstairs, the four bedrooms are generously sized with ensuite bathrooms and bay windows that overlook the gardens. The primary suite fills the western end of the house and offers a gas fireplace and two walk-in closets. The ensuite bath has a built-in soaking tub in one bay window and marble floor with inlaid design. Down the hall, two sizeable bedrooms, one with a fireplace, have angled bays facing south, and ensuite bathrooms. The substantial suite to the east has a marble fireplace, balcony, free-standing soaking tub, and pedestal sinks. A charming sitting room overlooks the front garden. A full-height attic adds two large bedrooms and one smaller bedroom, a full bath with double sinks, three bonus rooms and many closets. The lower floor, originally a ballroom, is now a family room with fireplace, entertainment center with surround sound, wet bar, wine cellar, pantry, half bath, laundry room, and storage. The former chauffeur’s quarters over the three-car garage is a studio apartment with kitchen and full bath. The plumbing, electrical, heating, security, entertainment, irrigation, and drainage systems have been upgraded throughout, and a new well supplies water for the gardens. A rch it e ct A lbe r t Fa r r designed this house in 1917, and contractor Alfred Peterson built it in 1918 for John Spohn, president of a wholesale food manufacturing and distribution company. Spohn may have built the house on speculation. He and his wife and two sons lived in it only three years. Businessman Bert C. Scott, of the Hall-Scott Motor Company, was the long-term resident. He and his wife Trubee, sons Kenneth R. and Edward B. (Bud) and daughter (Kathleen) lived there from 1920 to 1963. Scott partnered with engineer Elbert J. Hall and manufactured high performance internal combustion engines for aircraft, marine and truck engines. The Scotts were active socially and entertained frequently. In 1930, they won first prize for their outdoor Christmas tree decorated with silver tinsel and reflected in their front pond. Gail Lombardi is an architectural historian and President of the Piedmont Historical Society.

articles.text: Piedmont Scouts in Troop 6 had a couple of amazing adventures recently, with service projects and camping at Kirby Cove in the Marin Headlands and Angel Island. Both trips were centered on San Francisco Bay and the iconic Golden Gate Bridge. Troop 6 Scouts, based at Corpus Christi Church in Piedmont, value community service and actively look for opportunities to help in different ways. On February 26, they had the opportunity to help prepare campsites at Kirby Cove, located in the Marin Headlands and part of the Golden Gate National Recreation Area. It is a small site just west of the Golden Gate Bridge and includes five campsites as well as an old artillery battery from World War II. Since the site was closed during the COVID pandemic, there were two years’ worth of weeds and overgrowth to clear. The gravel pathways are designed for wheelchair access, so clearing them of debris and ivy was the top priority. The campsites had already been leveled with raised boxes for tents, but plants were encroaching onto the sites. With hoes, shovels, and brooms, a total of 15 Scouts and seven adults made good progress in rescuing the paths and sites from Mother Nature. In total, the troop was able to: • clear 700 feet of accessible trail • uncover eight buried campsite boundary markers • remove over 100 square feet of weeds from the campsites • sweep 380 square feet of pavement • remove five gallons of trash • clean two campsites of fallen debris After a hard day’s work, the Scouts drank in the spectacular views, spent time on the secluded beach watching cars cross over the bridge while ships crisscrossed below. After dinner, they hiked over a ridge to the Golden Gate Bridge, walked under the bridge, and enjoyed the moonlit views of Alcatraz and Angel islands. Alcatraz and the Zombie Hike The weekend of March 5-6 Troop 6 Scouts camped on the largest natural island in San Francisco Bay, Angel Island, known for its 740 acres of pristine parkland, picnic areas, hiking trails and its rich history as an immigration station from 1910 to 1940. The trip started at Corpus Christi Church on Saturday afternoon with 12 Scouts and three adults. After loading their camping gear, they boarded a ferry from Oakland to San Francisco’s Ferry building. From there, the group relaxed for the 50-minute ferry ride to Angel Island and then hiked about a mile and a quarter to a campsite close to the beach. This trip was aimed at teaching beginning backpacking skills. Scout patrols were given a “just add water” directive, which essentially meant that Scouts had to plan and prepare meals that only required water. The meals were rated on taste, use of ingredients and originality. As an extra twist, there was a “Pack it in, pack it out” challenge. Each patrol received a one-quart Ziploc bag to fit all the garbage they created including all packaging and any uneaten food. The patrols carried their Ziplocs out on Sunday to have them weighed at the next Troop meeting. After dinner and clean-up, the Scouts prepared for a Zombie hike. Armed with headlamps and flashlights they strode off into the dark. They hiked along the Troop 6 Scout Terry Pierre and Cub Scout Nicholas Pierre. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine has caused the largest refugee crisis in Europe since World War II, with reports of over 3 million Ukrainians fleeing their country. Brasfield chose Red Cross Ukraine and the Come Back Alive Fund, both of which provide vital aid to Ukrainians affected by armed conflict; including blood collection, mobilization of volunteers and resources, and emergency outreach. The Come Back Alive Fund was launched in 2014 when Russia annexed Crimea, largely considered the onset of the Russo-Ukraine conflict. Brasfield works for Grammarly, a cross-platform cloudbased typing assistant that uses artificial intelligence to review and correct spelling, grammar, and punctuation in digital writing. The company is based in San Francisco but was founded in Ukraine 12 years ago by Max Lytvyn, Alex Schevchenko, and Dmytro Lider. Grammarly Inc. maintains offices in Kyiv, the capital and most populous city of Ukraine that has experienced an extreme mass exodus due to the Russian invasion. She described the first-hand accounts as heartbreaking, which prompted her to search for ways to help from across the globe. “I’ve seen the support for Ukraine firsthand in Piedmont; Ukrainian flags proudly wave throughout my neighborhood, and bake sales are popping up right and left. Our bake sale took the guesswork out of properly vetting organizations,” she said. Brasfield noted that kids donated their ‘tooth fairy’ and birthday money, and parents bought cookies for entire soccer teams. She added that the bake sale’s success was a true testament to the generosity of Piedmont. “It was heartwarming to see the outpouring of support,” she said. “When I shared the fundraiser details with my colleagues in Ukraine, they cried.
